{"prompt": "How do I fix a wobbly bar stool leg without buying a new one?", "response": "First, flip the stool over and check if it's actually loose joints rather than an uneven leg — tighten every visible screw or bolt first, since that fixes most wobble on its own. If it's still wobbly, check for a genuinely short leg by setting the stool on a flat floor and seeing which leg lifts. For a short leg, self-adhesive felt pads stacked to the right thickness work well and stay hidden. For a loose wooden joint, remove the leg if possible, add wood glue into the joint, clamp it overnight, and reinsert. As a last resort, a small furniture leg leveler screwed into the bottom of the short leg gives adjustable height."}
{"prompt": "What's a basic method for making sourdough starter from scratch?", "response": "Day 1: Mix 50g whole wheat flour with 50g room-temp water in a jar, cover loosely, leave at room temp. Day 2 onward: Discard half the mixture, then feed with 50g flour (all-purpose is fine after day 2) and 50g water, stirring well, once daily. You'll likely see small bubbles by day 3-4 as wild yeast activates — this is normal and not yet 'ready.' By day 7-10, it should reliably double in size within 4-8 hours of feeding and smell pleasantly sour/yeasty rather than harsh. That doubling test is the real readiness signal, not just the number of days — trust the rise over the calendar."}

final_entries.prompt: How do I make a classic hollandaise sauce from scratch?
final_entries.response: Melt 1 stick (113g) unsalted butter and keep it warm — it should be hot but not bubbling. In a blender, combine 3 large egg yolks, 1 tbsp white wine vinegar, 1 tbsp water, and a pinch of cayenne. Pulse briefly, then with the motor running, slowly drizzle in the melted butter in a thin, steady stream. This emulsifies the sauce and takes about 1 minute. Season with ½ tsp salt and 1 tsp lemon juice. If it gets too thick, blend in a teaspoon of warm water. If it breaks (looks curdly), start again with 1 fresh yolk in the blender and slowly drizzle in the broken sauce. Serve immediately over eggs Benedict, asparagus, or fish.

final_entries.prompt: My drain is clogged and I don not want to use harsh chemicals. What should I try?
final_entries.response: Start simple: boil a kettle of water and slowly pour it down the drain — this melts grease blockages on its own in many cases. If that doesn not work, pour ½ cup baking powder (not soda) into the drain, wait 2 minutes, then add ½ cup white vinegar. It will fizz and expand, pushing against the clog. Let it sit 15 minutes, then flush with another kettle of boiling water. For stubborn clogs, a basic hand-crank plumber snake (available at any hardware store for around $10) can reach and break up debris further down the pipe than any pour-and-wait method. If water backs up from other drains in the same house, the blockage is in the main line and may need a professional.

final_entries.prompt: Can you give me a recipe for homemade pizza dough I can make tonight?
final_entries.response: Warm 1¼ cups water to about 110°F (just warm on your wrist). Stir in 2¼ tsp active dry yeast and 1 tsp sugar — wait 5 minutes until it foams. Add 3½ cups all-purpose flour, 2 tsp salt, and 2 tbsp olive oil. Mix with a wooden spoon until shaggy, then knead on a lightly floured surface for 8-10 minutes until smooth and elastic. The dough should spring back when you poke it. Place in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with a damp towel, and let rise in a warm spot for 1-1½ hours, until doubled. Punch down, divide into portions, and roll into your desired shape. Add sauce and toppings, bake at 475°F on a preheated pizza stone or inverted baking sheet for 10-13 minutes until the crust is golden.

final_entries.prompt: How do I properly water-propagate a pothos plant cutting?
final_entries.response: Cut a 6-inch stem from a healthy pothos vine just below a leaf node (the small bump where a leaf grows). Remove any leaves that would sit below the water line — only the top leaves should remain. Place the cutting in a clear glass or jar with about 2 inches of room-temperature water so the node is submerged but the leaves are not. Position the jar in bright, indirect light (a east-facing windowsill is ideal). Change the water every 5-7 days to prevent bacterial growth and keep the cutting fresh. Roots typically appear in 2-3 weeks starting as tiny white strands from the node. Once roots are 2-3 inches long, you can either keep it as a water plant — fertilizing monthly with diluted liquid plant food — or transplant it into potting soil.

final_entries.prompt: I need a quick recipe for a good vinaigrette that works with any salad.
final_entries.response: The golden ratio for any vinaigrette is 3 parts oil to 1 part acid. Start with 1 tbsp red wine vinegar (or apple cider vinegar, lemon juice, or champagne vinegar). Whisk it with ½ tsp Dijon mustard (the emulsifier that keeps it from separating), ½ tsp honey or maple syrup, and a pinch each of salt and pepper. Then slowly whisk in 3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, adding it drop by drop at first before increasing to a thin stream. Once thickened and emulsified, taste and adjust — more salt if it tastes flat, more acid if it is too rich. This keeps in a jar in the fridge for up to a week; just shake before using since the oil will separate from the cold.
